**Instructions.** Choose the single best answer (a–e) for each question. You may use a periodic table.
Calculators are allowed. Answers are rounded to the precision shown. Time yourself: aim for about 30 minutes
(roughly 2 minutes per question, the same pace as the full exam). **Solubility rules are not provided:** work from memory, as on the exam.

**Answer sheet.** Use the bubble answer sheet (`CHEM1301/exam-prep/answer-sheet/answer-sheet.pdf`), rows 1–15.

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```
**1.** What does the **net ionic equation** for a reaction in solution show?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Only the ions that stay dissolved\
b)\ The complete formulas of all reactants and products\
c)\ Only the spectator ions\
d)\ Only the components that are directly involved in the reaction, without spectator ions\
e)\ Every ion and compound present, including spectator ions

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```

**4.** Which solubility rule explains why CuCl~2~ is **soluble** in water?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Rule 4: most sulfates are soluble, except BaSO~4~, PbSO~4~, and CaSO~4~\
b)\ Rule 3: most chlorides are soluble, except AgCl, PbCl~2~, and Hg~2~Cl~2~\
c)\ Rule 2: most salts of Na^+^, K^+^, and NH~4~^+^ are soluble\
d)\ Rule 5: most hydroxides are only slightly soluble (NaOH and KOH are the exceptions)\
e)\ Rule 1: most nitrate (NO~3~^−^) salts are soluble

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```
**5.** Which solubility rule explains why FePO~4~ is **insoluble** in water?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Rule 5: most hydroxides are only slightly soluble (NaOH and KOH are the exceptions)\
b)\ Rule 4: most sulfates are soluble, except BaSO~4~, PbSO~4~, and CaSO~4~\
c)\ Rule 2: most salts of Na^+^, K^+^, and NH~4~^+^ are soluble\
d)\ Rule 6: most sulfides, carbonates, and phosphates are only slightly soluble\
e)\ Rule 1: most nitrate (NO~3~^−^) salts are soluble

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

**9.** Which is the balanced **molecular** equation for mixing aqueous Al(NO~3~)~3~ and KOH?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Al(NO~3~)~3~(aq) + 3KOH(aq) $\rightarrow$ Al(OH)~3~(aq) + 3KNO~3~(s)\
b)\ Al(NO~3~)~3~(aq) + 3KOH(aq) $\rightarrow$ Al(OH)~3~(s) + 3KNO~3~(aq)\
c)\ Al(NO~3~)~3~(aq) + KOH(aq) $\rightarrow$ Al(OH)~3~(s) + KNO~3~(aq)\
d)\ Al(NO~3~)~3~(aq) + KOH(aq) $\rightarrow$ AlOH(s) + KNO~3~(aq)\
e)\ No reaction (NR)

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```

**12.** Aqueous solutions of zinc nitrate and potassium phosphate are mixed. What is the **net ionic** equation?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ 3Zn^2+^(aq) + 6NO~3~^−^(aq) + 6K^+^(aq) + 2PO~4~^3−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ Zn~3~(PO~4~)~2~(s) + 6K^+^(aq) + 6NO~3~^−^(aq)\
b)\ Zn^2+^(aq) + PO~4~^3−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ Zn~3~(PO~4~)~2~(s)\
c)\ 3Zn^2+^(aq) + 2PO~4~^3−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ Zn~3~(PO~4~)~2~(s)\
d)\ No reaction occurs (NR)\
e)\ K^+^(aq) + NO~3~^−^(aq) $\rightarrow$ KNO~3~(s)

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```

```{=latex}
\needspace{9\baselineskip}
```

**15.** After writing the reactants as separated ions, what is the next step in predicting whether a precipitate forms when two ionic solutions are mixed?

```{=latex}
\begingroup\leftskip=1.5em
```
a)\ Balance the molecular equation\
b)\ Exchange the cations with the anions within the same salt\
c)\ Combine the two cations into one solid\
d)\ Cancel the spectator ions\
e)\ Exchange the anions of the two salts to find the solids that could form

```{=latex}
\par\endgroup\medskip
```
